variants.name: Node streams: write() -> false, wait for 'drain'
variants.implementation_notes: Node's flow control is a return-value protocol: Writable.write() returns false once the internal buffer passes highWaterMark, and the producer must stop writing until the 'drain' event fires; stream.pipeline() and Readable.pipe() wire the same handshake for whole graphs. The demand-driven simplification is async iteration (ES2018): `for await (const chunk of source)` pulls one chunk at a time, and an async generator's yield simply waits for the next pull, so no explicit queue is needed at all. Both replace the classic bounded-queue structure with platform buffering plus this signal - and neither helps if the signal is ignored.
pitfalls: Ignoring write()'s false keeps enqueuing into the writable until the process runs out of memory - the classic Node backpressure bug.
'drain' fires once the buffer is flushed; register the listener after the false return (once()) or a fast stream can miss the event and stall forever.
highWaterMark is a threshold, not a hard byte cap, and objectMode counts objects rather than bytes.
A stream that is never consumed (no reader, no pipe) buffers indefinitely; abandoned streams must be destroyed.

variants.name: Web Streams pull source with a queuing strategy
variants.implementation_notes: Web Streams invert the handshake: a ReadableStream with an underlying pull() source is only asked for data while there is room, the queuing strategy (CountQueuingStrategy/ByteLengthQueuingStrategy with highWaterMark) defines how much is 'enough', and controller.desiredSize exposes the remaining capacity to the source. That makes backpressure declarative - you describe the queue and the platform pulls only when the consumer reads - and it replaces the classic bounded queue in browsers and in Node's webstreams. The WritableStream side mirrors it: writer.write() returns a promise that settles when the chunk is accepted, and writer.ready reflects the queue pressure of the sink.
pitfalls: A pull source that ignores desiredSize (or enqueues in its own loop instead of in pull) has an unbounded queue and no backpressure.
desiredSize goes negative when the internal queue exceeds highWaterMark - a signal to stop, not a byte count that can be written.
Converting between web and Node streams (Readable.fromWeb/toWeb) requires a reader/writer to be attached or the handshake is lost and the queue grows.
An unread ReadableStream keeps whatever the source pumped into it alive; cancel() or consume it.
